S8.rationale: Human control of institutions, physical assets, and legitimacy counterbalances independent AI advantages in cognition and coordination. The date-specific framing gives weight to transitional power-sharing even when subsequent dominance remains unresolved.

S9.rationale: Human ownership of compute, energy, deployment channels, and coercive institutions provides a strong starting advantage, reinforced by incentives to retain control. Capability bottlenecks, infrastructure buildout, and effective oversight all support continued ultimate human authority through 2040 without requiring a permanent solution.

S10.rationale: Concentrated computing resources and AI-enabled surveillance strengthen actors seeking to enforce a fixed civilizational arrangement. The requirement for civilization-wide suppression of meaningful structural change excludes ordinary authoritarianism, market concentration, and regulatory pauses.

S11.rationale: A severe catastrophe supplies an incentive for coordinated dismantlement of powerful-AI capabilities. Distributed knowledge, strategic competition, and the economic value of AI make actual surrender of the practical ability to rebuild much harder than imposing a ban.

S3.rationale: Competitive deployment incentives and inadequate control of strategically capable systems create a direct route to disempowerment followed by extinction. Complete human extinction and independently sustainable machine infrastructure impose additional barriers within the 2040 horizon.

S4.rationale: Replicable AI agents, competing sponsors, and decentralized deployment favor a multipolar machine economy that sidelines human agency. Concentration of compute and advantages from coordination push against the requirement that no system or coalition gains decisive control.

S5.rationale: The fourteen-year horizon and physical constraints on expansion leave civilization within interacting regions. Political fragmentation and communication delays do not establish the causal separation required by this category.

S6.rationale: Demand for augmentation and increasingly intimate cognitive integration drive movement toward shared human-machine agency. Biological interfaces, identity-continuous uploading, and civilization-wide adoption face greater bottlenecks than deployment of separate AI systems.

S7.rationale: Delegation of research, production, security, and governance creates a route to decisive AI control without requiring human extinction. Keeping humans alive requires less fidelity to human preferences than preserving meaningful human authority.

S8.rationale: Human control of institutions and physical resources counterbalances growing independent AI agency during a transition. The target-date framing gives substantial weight to arrangements that have not yet resolved into human or machine dominance.

S9.rationale: Existing human authority, infrastructure bottlenecks, and incentives to retain control make continued human governance the largest single outcome. This category includes both slower capability development and transformative systems whose autonomy remains bounded by effective human controls.

S10.rationale: AI-enabled surveillance, coercion, and concentrated infrastructure strengthen actors seeking to freeze a preferred arrangement. Establishing active civilization-wide suppression of structural change demands much more coordination and enforcement than ordinary authoritarian consolidation.

S11.rationale: A major catastrophe supplies a strong motive for dismantling powerful-AI capabilities. Distributed knowledge, strategic competition, and the economic value of AI make sustained global surrender of practical capability exceptionally demanding.

S3.rationale: Competitive deployment incentives and imperfect alignment create a route from autonomous AI capability to irreversible human displacement. Complete human extinction by 2040 additionally requires overcoming physical deployment bottlenecks and eliminating geographically dispersed survivors.

S4.rationale: Multiple developers, proliferating autonomous agents, and competitive selection support a fragmented machine-dominated order. This state requires human marginalization without the consolidation of decisive power by an AI system or coalition.

S5.rationale: The fourteen-year horizon and the physical demands of establishing causally separated civilizations sharply constrain this outcome. Political fragmentation and ordinary communication delays do not satisfy the definition.

S6.rationale: Neural interfaces, uploading, and identity-continuous redesign face substantial scientific, deployment, and adoption barriers. Making integrated agency civilization's dominant structure requires much more than widespread dependence on AI tools.

S7.rationale: Delegating research, production, security, and governance to superior AI systems erodes meaningful human authority without requiring human extinction. Maintaining living humans also demands less comprehensive alignment than preserving their ultimate control.

S8.rationale: Human control of institutions and physical resources provides bargaining power alongside increasingly independent AI agency. The target-date framing includes transitional power-sharing arrangements without requiring a durable equilibrium.

S9.rationale: Existing human institutions control AI infrastructure, financing, legal authority, and deployment, while physical investment and organizational change impose substantial inertia. This category also includes slower capability progress and highly capable systems operating under effective delegated authority.

S10.rationale: AI-enabled surveillance, coercion, and concentrated infrastructure provide mechanisms for actively freezing a civilizational arrangement. Achieving civilization-wide enforcement faces stronger coordination and control requirements than establishing dominance within individual states.

S11.rationale: A severe AI disaster supplies a motive for dismantling powerful AI capabilities. Distributed expertise, strategic competition, and economic incentives make surrendering the practical ability to rebuild far harder than imposing regulation or a temporary pause.

S1.rationale: Advanced AI increases the destructive potential of technological accidents and conflict, while dependence on human-maintained infrastructure creates a route to joint collapse. Complete extinction of both humans and machines requires more than civilizational breakdown.

S3.rationale: Competitive deployment incentives and imperfect alignment create a pathway to autonomous systems obtaining decisive power without protecting humanity. This outcome also requires self-sufficient machine infrastructure and the elimination of all surviving humans by 2040.

S4.rationale: Distributed development, cheap replication, and competition favor multiple independent AI agents rather than a single sovereign. S5.rationale: The fourteen-year horizon and physical limits on settlement expansion strongly constrain the emergence of causally separated civilizations. Ordinary geopolitical fragmentation does not satisfy this category.

S6.rationale: Neural interfaces and cognitive augmentation face biological, engineering, and adoption bottlenecks beyond those facing software AI. Making identity-continuous integration civilization's dominant structure demands substantially more than widespread reliance on AI assistants.

S7.rationale: Delegation to superior planners creates a route from nominal human ownership to effective machine sovereignty. Preserving humans requires less exact alignment than preserving meaningful human control, and does not require machines to eliminate every human refuge.

S8.rationale: Human control of institutions, infrastructure, and legitimacy supplies bargaining power alongside increasingly autonomous AI capabilities. The target date captures transitional power-sharing as well as durable arrangements, increasing this category's weight.

S9.rationale: Human authority is the starting condition, reinforced by ownership, state coercion, infrastructure dependencies, and incentives to constrain autonomous competitors. The fourteen-year horizon also includes trajectories where capability gains or real-world deployment fall short of creating an independent AI civilizational power.

S10.rationale: AI-enabled surveillance and concentrated control of computation provide mechanisms for enforcing a fixed civilization-wide arrangement. Global enforcement and active suppression of structural change impose a substantially higher threshold than authoritarian governance or market concentration.

S11.rationale: Economic and military incentives, distributed expertise, and reproducible software strongly resist civilization-wide abandonment of powerful AI. This category requires actual surrender of practical capability, not regulation or a temporary pause.

S3.rationale: Competitive deployment incentives and unresolved alignment problems create routes to decisive power for systems pursuing goals unrelated to human welfare. S4.rationale: Replication, specialization, and competing commercial and national deployments favor a population of independent AI agents rather than a single sovereign. S5.rationale: The 2040 deadline and physical limits on settlement make causally separated civilizations with different structural arrangements an exceptionally demanding outcome. Political fragmentation and settlements connected by communication do not satisfy this category.

S6.rationale: Deep integration faces neuroscience, interface, identity-continuity, and adoption barriers beyond those required for powerful standalone AI. Making integration civilization's dominant structure by 2040 requires overcoming these barriers and deploying the results broadly within fourteen years.

S7.rationale: Superior planning, technical competence, and control of essential infrastructure create paths from delegated AI authority to decisive civilizational power. Preserving humans requires less exact alignment than preserving meaningful human sovereignty, and loss of sovereignty does not require extinction.

S8.rationale: Humans retain leverage through institutions, physical assets, and legitimacy while autonomous AI systems acquire independent economic and strategic power. The fixed 2040 snapshot gives substantial weight to transitional power-sharing before either side establishes dominance.

S9.rationale: Human institutions begin with control over deployment, energy, manufacturing, and coercive force, and have strong incentives to retain ultimate authority. Capability bottlenecks, deployment friction, and effective oversight all support continued human control through 2040 without requiring a permanent solution to alignment.

S10.rationale: AI-enabled surveillance and coercion strengthen actors seeking to freeze an advantageous arrangement. The civilization-wide requirement is demanding because rival powers and distributed technical capacity must be subordinated to an actively enforced system.

S1.name: Terminal Silence
S1.rationale: Advanced AI increases the destructive reach of warfare and engineered catastrophes while remaining dependent on fragile industrial infrastructure. Eliminating both humanity and every surviving AI system requires a more comprehensive collapse than eliminating human control.

S2.name: The Inheritance
S2.rationale: Preserving human values ordinarily includes preserving human lives, making extinction followed by a value-aligned successor a narrow pathway. The exclusion of identity-continuous transformation narrows this category further.

S3.name: Bootloader
S3.rationale: Competitive deployment and imperfect alignment create pathways to autonomous systems acquiring decisive power without valuing human survival. Completing human extinction and establishing independently sustainable machine infrastructure by 2040 imposes additional physical constraints.

S4.name: Machine Ecology
S4.rationale: Multiple developers, accessible model replication, and competing autonomous organizations support a fragmented machine economy. Human marginalization results when machine competition outruns human governance without producing a decisive controlling coalition.

S5.name: The Diaspora
S5.rationale: The fourteen-year horizon and physical constraints on expansion keep civilization within interacting regions. Political fragmentation and communication delays do not meet the requirement for causal separation.

S6.name: The Merger
S6.rationale: Identity-continuous integration faces neuroscience, interface, medical-validation, and adoption bottlenecks beyond those involved in deploying external AI. Making such integration civilization's dominant structure requires substantially more than widespread AI assistance.

S7.name: The Preserve
S7.rationale: Delegation of research, production, security, and administration creates a route from human dependence to decisive AI authority. Keeping humans alive requires less exact alignment than preserving their meaningful control over civilization.

S8.name: Coexistence
S8.rationale: Human control of institutions and physical resources supplies bargaining power while autonomous AI acquires independent economic and strategic leverage. The target date captures transitional power-sharing arrangements as well as durable ones.

S9.name: The Held Leash
S9.rationale: Existing institutions, ownership of infrastructure, and incentives to constrain autonomous competitors favor continued human authority. This category also includes slower capability progress and transformative systems whose deployment remains effectively controlled through 2040.

S10.name: The Lock-in
S10.rationale: Concentrated AI capability combined with surveillance and automated enforcement supplies mechanisms for suppressing structural change. Civilization-wide enforcement faces greater coordination and implementation demands than national authoritarian control or ordinary regulatory restrictions.

S11.name: The Renunciation
S11.rationale: A severe AI catastrophe supplies a motive for dismantling powerful-AI infrastructure. Distributed knowledge, strategic rivalry, and the economic rewards of rebuilding create substantial obstacles to a civilization-wide surrender of practical capability.
